title: Redwood discovery - Veridian Payments - latency & throughput
summary: Discovery call to understand Veridian's latency SLAs (p95 targets), expected concurrency, streaming requirements and feasibility of hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Customer interested in running token/sec benchmarks and a short POC with dedicated capacity. Security and data residency are key blockers (VPC/KMS/SOC2).
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood, AE on the account. Jordan, our SE, and I will run through your latency and throughput needs. quick intro?
[00:12] Alex: Yup, Alex Chen here, CTO at Veridian Payments. We build real-time fraud scoring and tokenization APIs. Time is critical, so latency is the big one.
[00:22] Priya: Priya, lead ML. I'm focused on model quality and inference perf, we do streaming for step-by-step scoring and also batch inference for offline.
[00:30] Mike: Mike, infra lead, want to understand networking, VPC options and how tokens/sec maps to our node sizing.
[00:40] Jordan: great. quick agenda — collect p95 targets, concurrency, streaming patterns, and then discuss hosting options (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and what a benchmark POC would look like.
[00:55] Samira: just to set expectations, we often recommend starting with a dedicated pilot for predictable latency; hosted good if you want fastest time to value, private for strict compliance.
[01:10] Alex: our hard requirement is p95 < 120ms for 256-token prompts in the happy path. Under load we accept graceful degradation but want 99th < 300ms ideally.
[01:25] Jordan: ok p95 <120ms for 256 tokens — that's tight but feasible on optimized runtimes. can i ask what model family you're evaluating and whether you need streaming?
[01:37] Priya: we're experimenting with open weights — mixture of Llama2 family and some smaller instruction-tuned models. We definitely use streaming for multi-turn scoring (we stream partial decisions).
[01:50] Jordan: streaming adds a little more complexity because you want low time-to-first-token and then sustained throughput. Are you doing synchronous requests per user (low concurrency) or large concurrent request spikes?
[02:05] Alex: both. typical concurrency is 50-200 concurrent real-time requests during peak; we have spikes to 800 for marketing bursts. Each request is short (100-600 tokens) but we need first token under 50ms ideally.
[02:20] Mike: and network is across us-east and eu-west, data residency for payments can be us-only for certain flows. we need VPC peering for private deployment.
[02:34] Samira: good context. From a Redwood perspective we can route requests regionally and pin workloads. For your first-token under 50ms — on dedicated instances with optimized kernels and warm KV cache that's plausible. On hosted, depends on cold starts and underlying tenancy.
[02:54] Jordan: yes, we typically separate two metrics: time-to-first-token (TTFT) and p95 token completion. For models like 3B-13B family tuned, with continuous batching and prefix KV cache we often hit p95 in the 80-140ms range for 256 tokens on dedicated NVIDIA A10x or similar, but YMMV.
[03:20] Priya: when you say batching, does that increase latency? our spikes are bursty and we can't buffer requests for too long.
[03:28] Jordan: continuous batching is workload-aware; it batches opportunistically within latency SLOs. For strict 50ms TTFT targets we can disable batching for those routes and use single-request fast paths; cost goes up but latency stabilizes.
[03:42] Alex: cost is a factor. What's the unit economics difference between hosted and dedicated for our workload?
[03:48] Samira: i'll send a pricing baseline after this call — dedicated is committed price with reserved capacity which makes high concurrency cheaper; hosted is pay-as-you-go — for steady high concurrency dedicated usually wins. We'll include token/sec and per-GPU throughput numbers in the deck.
[04:05] Mike: about benchmarking — Priya and i want to run an in-house tokens/sec benchmark that mirrors our real request distribution. can Redwood run a side-by-side with our workload?
[04:16] Jordan: absolutely. typical POC is 1) we provision a dedicated pool matching your concurrency (e.g., N GPUs), 2) you run a playback of your traffic, 3) we measure p95, TTFT, tokens/sec, and tail latency with streaming enabled. We can also test quantized model variants.
[04:36] Priya: how long would that POC need to be? we can allocate infra for 2 weeks.
[04:41] Jordan: 1 week can be enough for initial benchmarks but 2 weeks is better for stability and warm caches — so your 2-week window is perfect.
[04:52] Alex: what telemetry do we get? we need token-level cost breakdowns and tracing to tie request ids back to logs.
[04:59] Samira: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, tracing hooks, and KV cache hit rates. We'll share the dashboard access during the POC.
[05:12] Mike: security — we require SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, and that customer keys are in our KMS. can you support customer-managed KMS and an on-prem private control plane?
[05:24] Jordan: yes — for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integration and an air-gapped option. Dedicated also supports VPC peering and customer KMS for encryption at rest. Hosted can use envelope encryption with BYOK in many cases.
[05:40] Priya: network latency between us and the Redwood endpoint will obviously matter. can you provide suggested deployment topologies for minimal RTT?
[05:49] Samira: recommended is colocating dedicated pools in the same cloud region as your app frontends (we support regions in us-east-1 and eu-west-1). For Private, you can run inference in your VPC to eliminate cross-account hops. We'll share a network diagram.
[06:05] Alex: ok circling back to numbers — can you give an example baseline: 256 tokens, 200 concurrency, p95 target 120ms — what GPU count and model size do we need?
[06:18] Jordan: rough thumb rule: for streaming-friendly 13B models at 200 concurrency you might need 4-6 high-memory GPUs (A100s or H100 equivalents) depending on sequence length and KV cache hits. For 3B models you can fit many more QPS per GPU. We will size more accurately after we run your tokens/sec profile.
[06:42] Mike: if we use quantized 4-bit models, do we see large hit to quality? our tolerance is modest, we need true positive rates unchanged by more than 1-2%.
[06:51] Priya: yes, model quality is non-negotiable for fraud detection.
[06:55] Jordan: quantization can be a win; with per-workload evals we often find 4-bit QAT or PTQ keeps metrics within 1% for many models. We'll include quality regression monitoring in the POC.
[07:10] Alex: on the topic of fallbacks — if a dedicated pool is saturated do you fallback to hosted or lower-tier model variants?
[07:18] Samira: yes, routing policies can fallback to cheaper model variants or other regions. We can set canary/auto-fallback rules to avoid 503s.
[07:27] Mike: about metrics collection — we want Prometheus-compatible metrics, plus tracing.
[07:33] Jordan: Redwood can stream metrics to your telemetry backend; we also expose Prom-compatible endpoints and distribute tracing headers to link requests.
[07:43] Priya: for the benchmark payload — we have multi-turn sessions where partial tokens feed back; can you replicate streaming token-by-token?
[07:51] Jordan: yes we can drive token-level streaming with our benchmark harness to measure time-per-token and average tokens/sec per GPU.
[08:00] Samira: two clarifying items — target p95 of 120ms and first token under 50ms for certain routes, concurrency typical 50-200, spikes to 800, need region pinning and VPC/KMS for compliance. Did I capture that?
[08:13] Alex: yeah that's right, with the note that some flows must be US-only.
[08:19] Mike: and we want dashboarding and token-level cost in the POC.
[08:23] Samira: great. let's talk scope and next steps for POC. Jordan?
[08:28] Jordan: ideal POC: dedicated pool in us-east pinned to your traffic, 2-week run, we'll test 3B and 13B variants, quantized and FP16, streaming enabled, run your traffic replay, measure p95/TTFT/tokens-per-second and quality regression on your eval prompts. We'll also test fallback routing.
[08:46] Priya: sounds good. what's the data flow for POC — do we need to send data to Redwood?
[08:52] Samira: not necessary if you use a playback harness that runs from your env. But for deeper tests we can deploy a private data plane in your VPC so tokens never leave your network. For hosted/dedicated the inference plane may be in Redwood-managed infra, but you can opt for Private for strict data residency.
[09:10] Alex: timeframe — we can start the POC mid-March.
[09:14] Samira: ok I'll propose dates. Any blockers?
[09:18] Mike: procurement and security review. we'll need SOC2 docs, network diagrams, and a standard MSA addendum for dedicated capacity.
[09:26] Samira: we'll send SOC2, architecture, privacy and sample MSA addendum.
[09:31] Priya: on benchmarks — i want tokens/sec numbers per GPU for 3B vs 13B with streaming. can you include those in the perf runbook?
[09:40] Jordan: yes, sample numbers: rough order — 3B can do ~1.2-1.8k tokens/sec per A10x-ish GPU with streaming optimizations, 13B more like 300-700 tokens/sec depending on quantization and prompt length. we'll provide a more precise table after we profile your payload.
[10:03] Alex: those are helpful. question: for first-token under 50ms do you have any hardened configs?
[10:10] Jordan: fast-path configs: keep model warmed, pre-allocate KV cache, disable batching on that route, and pin to single-tenant GPUs. That combination reduces scheduling and kernel initialization.
[10:24] Priya: also curious about cold start behavior — how long to ramp to warm performance after a burst?
[10:30] Jordan: typically seconds to a minute; depends on model size and cache warming. For continuous live traffic caches warm faster. We monitor warm-hit rates in console.
[10:41] Mike: network jitter might add 20-30ms sometimes. Factor that into SLOs.
[10:46] Samira: noted. we'll include network guidance and a recommended SLO buffer.
[10:52] Alex: ok do you have an example benchmark report from another payments customer?
[10:58] Samira: i can share a redacted report with tokens/sec, p95, TTFT and cost. we'll redact names.
[11:04] Priya: great. for the POC, can Redwood run model quantization and provide checkpoints, or do we need to do that ourselves?
[11:12] Jordan: we can assist with quantization and can provide quantized variants for testing; we'll also run evals to check regressions.
[11:18] Alex: what about canarying - if we roll to production, do you offer A/B and automatic rollback?
[11:24] Samira: yes, redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B comparisons and automatic fallback policies based on latency or error budget.
[11:32] Mike: procurement question — for dedicated do you need an annual commit?
[11:35] Samira: we offer monthly reserved capacity or annual for discounts. for a pilot you can do a short-term reserved pool. We'll include options in the pricing.
[11:46] Alex: ok let's document next steps and owners.
[11:50] Samira: Jordan, can you run the perf runbook and sizing template and assist with POC setup?
[11:55] Jordan: yes, i'll prepare the runbook and a sizing spreadsheet.
[11:58] Samira: i'll send pricing and SOC2/docs. Priya, can you prepare a masked playback dataset and traffic profile?
[12:05] Priya: yes, we can provide a synthetic replay with production-like distributions and redacted tokens.
[12:10] Samira: Alex/Mike, procurement attach point for legal — who should i cc?
[12:15] Alex: cc me and Mike.
[12:18] Samira: great, we'll follow up. thanks everyone.
[12:22] Alex: thanks, bye.
